structure.title: The Last Day – The Philosopher and Death · A friend remembers the last day
structure.text: Phaedo describes the prison to a man who was absent. Before the arguments begin we know that somebody had to carry them out of the room, along with memories of tears, laughter and the removal of Socrates' chains.

structure.title: The Argument from Opposites – The Affinity Argument · Several ways a soul might survive
structure.text: Socrates tries opposites, recollection and the soul's resemblance to things that hold their shape through change. The arguments answer different questions. Having existed before the body, for instance, leaves open what becomes of the soul after death.

structure.title: The Objections – The Death of Socrates · The objections reach the bedside
structure.text: Two friends voice the difficulties everyone would prefer to spare a dying man. Socrates welcomes them, tells how his own search for causes went wrong and offers another argument before the practical business of dying returns.

people.name: Simmias
people.role: The friend with a musical objection
people.text: A tuned instrument produces a harmony more elusive than wood or strings. Breaking the instrument can still destroy the harmony. The example puts pressure on an argument from the soul's invisible character to its durability.

people.name: Cebes
people.role: The friend who imagines a weaver
people.text: A weaver can outlast many cloaks and still die before the last wears out. Cebes grants Socrates considerably more than Simmias does and shows why even that concession leaves the central question unsettled.

prerequisites.title: Plato's Apology
prerequisites.text: The Phaedo takes place on the day of Socrates' death. The Apology is his defence at the trial that condemned him, where he tells the jury why death need not be feared; the Phaedo puts that calm to the test.

context.title: What counts as a cause?
context.text: Bones and muscles make it physically possible for Socrates to sit in prison. His decision to accept the sentence explains why he is sitting here today. This homely distinction helps make sense of the dialogue's demanding late turn toward explanation.

notice.text: Notice who is afraid to speak.
notice.why: Tenderness can tempt the friends to withhold an objection. The room makes clear what honest inquiry can cost people who care deeply about the answer and about one another.
Phaedo remembers how an argument felt when it appeared to collapse. A listener's loss of heart becomes an event that needs attention before any proof can resume.

opening: Socrates' friends arrive at the prison knowing he will die that day. He wants to discuss whether death should frighten them, and whether the soul can survive the body. They listen, object, and worry that affection is making them too willing to believe him. Plato places an argument about immortality beside the immediate business of losing a friend. Every objection carries two pressures at once: the need for an answer that holds up, and the wish that it might offer consolation before time runs out.
